chapterTitle: Dependency Injection (DI) and Inversion of Control (IoC) with Creational Patterns
aiGenerationNote: Create a 15-minute video walkthrough demonstrating Dependency Injection in a Spring Boot project. Start by showing a tightly coupled example without DI. Then, introduce an interface `DataService` and two implementations (`JdbcDataService`, `MockDataService`). Demonstrate constructor injection in a `ReportService` that depends on `DataService`. Use `@Component` and `@Autowired` (on constructor) to let Spring manage the dependencies. Show how easily you can swap implementations by changing a single `@Bean` definition or profile. Include terminal output showing the Spring context starting up and the beans being created. Visually highlight the `@Component` and constructor injection points in the code. End with a mini-quiz asking about the benefits of DI for testability.

screens.title: Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll unpack two foundational ideas that modern Java frameworks use to keep large codebases clean and testable. Inversion of Control is a design principle where the framework, not your classes, decides when and how components are created and called. Dependency Injection is the practical mechanism that supplies an object with the other objects it needs to do its work. Together they shift responsibility for object creation to an external container, which improves modularity, simplifies testing, and reduces direct coupling between classes. You will see a concrete example with a UserService and a UserRepository, and we will contrast manual ‘new’ construction with container-managed creation. We will also explain constructor, setter, and field injection, and how DI containers map to creational patterns like Factory and Singleton so you can reason about object scope and lifecycle. By the end of this chapter you will know how DI changes where object wiring happens, why constructor injection is usually preferred, and the common pitfalls to avoid when using container-managed singletons or field injection. Consider how handing over control to a container changes the responsibilities of your classes and what that means for testing and substitutability.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Dependency Injection
Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control
How DI implements IoC and complements creational patterns in Java
In this lesson
Learn IoC and DI definitions, DI types, how Spring manages beans, and how DI maps to Factory and Singleton patterns.
Why it matters
Shifting creation to a container makes code modular and testable. You can swap implementations without changing consumer code.
Explore Key Topics
IoC Principle
Framework-invoked control that decouples flow from application code.
DI Types
Constructor, setter, and field injection and their trade-offs.
DI & Patterns
How containers act like factories and manage singleton scope for you.

A container creates beans, resolves dependencies, and injects them where needed.
Bean: UserRepository
Bean: UserService (depends on UserRepository)
Container wires them at startup
Quick example
A UserService that receives a UserRepository from outside is easier to replace in tests than one that constructs it directly.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will do four practical things that matter when building maintainable Java code. First, you will define Inversion of Control and explain how moving control to a container decouples components; this helps you reason about where responsibilities belong. Second, you will understand Dependency Injection as the implementation of IoC and list its benefits such as improved testability and reduced coupling, with clear examples that show how to replace a concrete repository with a mock. Third, you will identify constructor, setter, and field injection, and describe practical trade-offs so you can choose the safest option for required versus optional dependencies. Fourth, you will explain how DI containers like Spring manage creation, injection, and lifecycle, and relate that to creational patterns like Factory and Singleton so you can predict object scope and lifecycle. Each objective equips you to make design choices and avoid common mistakes such as over-injecting or misusing singleton scope. Let's look at the competency cards you will master.

screens.title: Inversion of Control (IoC)
screens.narratorSegment: Inversion of Control is a design principle that flips who decides what happens in your application. Instead of your classes instantiating and orchestrating every dependency, a framework or container takes responsibility for calling into your components and creating them as needed. That change in control decouples the flow of your application from the specific implementations of its parts. For example, rather than a service asking for a repository with new, the framework constructs the repository and supplies it when the service is created. This matters because it reduces the knowledge each class needs about other classes, making them easier to test and replace. A common misconception is that IoC means removing all application logic; it does not. IoC only transfers responsibility for object lifecycle and wiring to the container; domain behavior still lives in your classes. A helpful analogy is a stage production: imagine the container as the stage manager who cues actors (your components), while the actors focus on their script. Practically, IoC leads to clearer boundaries between configuration and behavior, and it enables features like lifecycle callbacks and scoped instances. Reflect on whether a class should create its own collaborators or instead expose the collaborators it needs, so the container can supply them.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Inversion of Control (IoC)
Definition
IoC hands control over object creation and calling to an external container instead of internal code.
Analogy: Container as stage manager that cues actors
Why it matters: Separates configuration/wiring from behavior for easier testing.
Misconception: IoC does not remove domain logic; it only changes who wires objects.
Key Takeaway
Think in terms of roles: containers manage lifecycle and wiring; classes implement behavior and declare what they need.
Concrete scenario
Compare: an application that calls new to create a repository vs one where the container creates the repository and injects it into the service. The latter lets you replace implementations without changing the consumer code.
Check your understanding
  • Identify which responsibilities move to the container under IoC.
  • Explain how IoC reduces coupling and improves testability.
  • Give an example where IoC enables swapping an implementation in tests.

screens.title: Dependency Injection (DI)
screens.narratorSegment: Dependency Injection is a specific way to implement Inversion of Control by supplying an object's collaborators from the outside. The central claim is simple: a class should declare what it needs and let someone else provide it. That makes the class modular and easier to test. To make this concrete, compare two implementations of a UserService. In the tightly coupled version the service constructs its own UserRepository. This forces the service to know about a particular implementation and prevents easy substitution. In the injected version the UserRepository is provided in the constructor. This lets tests supply a mock implementation or swap in a different persistence strategy without changing the service. A common pitfall is over-using DI to inject too many responsibilities into a single class; if a constructor grows long, it may indicate a design problem. Another misconception is that DI removes coupling entirely — it reduces implementation coupling but introduces configuration coupling via the container. In practice DI improves maintainability: you change wiring once in the configuration rather than modifying many classes. As a takeaway, whenever a class talks about 'new' for collaborators, ask whether those collaborators belong in a container instead.

keyIdea.title: DI in practice
keyIdea.text: Declare dependencies; let the container provide them to reduce implementation coupling and enable swapping in tests.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Dependency Injection (DI)
Tight coupling (no DI)
// Without DI - Tight Coupling
public class UserService {
  private UserRepository userRepository;

  public UserService() {
    this.userRepository = new UserRepositoryImpl(); // creates its own dependency
  }

  public User getUserById(Long id) {
    return userRepository.findById(id);
  }
}
This version hardcodes the concrete repository and resists replacement in tests.
Constructor injection (DI)
// With DI - Constructor Injection
public class UserService {
  private final UserRepository userRepository;

  public UserService(UserRepository userRepository) { // dependency provided from outside
    this.userRepository = userRepository;
  }

  public User getUserById(Long id) {
    return userRepository.findById(id);
  }
}
This version accepts any implementation that fulfills the UserRepository contract, making substitution and mocking straightforward.
Benefit: Easier testing and swapability
Pitfall: Too many injected dependencies may indicate poor design
Misconception: DI removes all coupling; it only shifts it to configuration

screens.title: DI Types: Constructor, Setter, Field
screens.narratorSegment: There are three widely used styles of dependency injection, and each has trade-offs you should know. Constructor injection provides dependencies through a class constructor and is preferred for required collaborators because it guarantees a fully initialized object and promotes immutability. For example, a NotificationService that requires a MessageService should declare it in the constructor so you cannot create the notification service without the message service. Setter injection supplies dependencies via public setter methods. This works well for optional dependencies or when you need to change a collaborator after construction, but it requires null checks or runtime checks to ensure correctness. Field injection places dependencies directly into private fields using framework support, for example with annotations in Spring. It is concise but reduces testability because it bypasses constructors and setters, making manual instantiation harder. A common misconception is that field injection is always fine for small projects; in unit testing scenarios constructor injection reduces setup complexity. Also avoid 'constructor hell' where a single class has many constructor parameters—this is usually a symptom that the class has too many responsibilities. As a takeaway, prefer constructor injection for required dependencies, setter injection for optional ones, and reserve field injection for framework-managed components where constructor wiring is impractical.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › DI Types: Constructor, Setter, Field
Constructor Injection
Dependencies come through the constructor. Best for required collaborators and immutability.
public class NotificationService {
  private final MessageService messageService;

  public NotificationService(MessageService messageService) {
    this.messageService = messageService;
  }
}
Advantage: object created in a valid state. Pitfall: very long constructors signal design issues.
Setter Injection
Optional dependencies are supplied via setters; useful for mutable or optional collaborators.
public class UserService {
  private UserRepository userRepository;

  public void setUserRepository(UserRepository userRepository) {
    this.userRepository = userRepository;
  }
}
Remember to validate optional dependencies before use.
Field Injection
Dependencies are injected directly into fields with annotations. Concise but harder to unit test outside the container.
public class UserService {
  @Autowired
  private UserRepository userRepository;
}
Use field injection sparingly; prefer constructor injection for testability.

screens.title: DI Container Responsibilities
screens.narratorSegment: A DI container performs four essential responsibilities that shape how your application behaves. First, it creates object instances for classes registered as beans or components. Second, it resolves dependencies by inspecting constructor parameters, setter methods, or field annotations and determining which beans satisfy those contracts. Third, it injects resolved dependencies into the target objects so the objects can operate without creating their own collaborators. Fourth, it manages object lifecycle, which includes singleton default scope, optional prototype scope, and lifecycle callbacks like initialization and destruction. These responsibilities map directly to creational patterns: the container behaves like a central Factory that decides when to call factory methods or construct objects, and like a managed Singleton registry when it provides a single shared instance for a bean. A common misunderstanding is that the container replaces design patterns; instead, it complements them by centralizing creation and reducing boilerplate. Practically, knowing these responsibilities helps you predict when objects are instantiated, when shared state might occur, and how to configure scopes to avoid unintended sharing. When designing components, assume the container will construct and wire them, and keep classes focused on behavior rather than creation.

keyIdea.title: Container role
keyIdea.text: Create, resolve, inject, and manage lifecycle of application objects; act as a managed factory and singleton manager.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › DI Container Responsibilities
Four container responsibilities
1
Object creation
Container constructs beans using constructors or factory methods.
2
Dependency resolution
Container decides which bean fulfills each dependency contract.
3
Dependency injection
Container injects dependencies via constructor, setter, or field.
4
Lifecycle management
Container applies scopes and lifecycle callbacks for bean instances.
Practical note: when you see unexpected shared state, check bean scope and where the container creates the instance.
Container as patterns
Treat the container as a central Factory and a managed Singleton registry. You still use other creational patterns where they fit, but the container reduces boilerplate by centralizing creation and wiring.
Check your thinking
  • When does the container create a bean? At startup for singleton beans, or on demand for prototype beans.
  • How does container-managed singleton differ from a class-level singleton implementation?

screens.title: Creational Patterns vs DI Containers
screens.narratorSegment: Creational patterns remain useful even when you adopt DI, but a container often takes over their roles. The Factory Method pattern encapsulates object creation in a method; when you annotate @Bean or use configuration, the container calls a factory method on your behalf. The Singleton pattern enforces a single instance at the class level, but a DI container provides a more flexible managed singleton: the container controls singularity and can swap implementations for testing. The Builder pattern still applies when constructing complex value or configuration objects; the container can inject a fully built object rather than assembling it itself. A common misconception is that DI obviates these patterns entirely; instead DI often reduces boilerplate by centralizing creation while the patterns remain the right tool for constructing particular object families or complex instances. For example, a @Configuration class that defines a userRepository bean is conceptually a factory method. If you need a complex HttpClient, using a Builder to configure it before injection keeps your services simple and the configuration explicit. As a takeaway, view the container as an orchestrator that can call your factory methods and manage scopes, allowing creational patterns and DI to complement each other.

keyIdea.title: Patterns complement DI
keyIdea.text: Containers often implement Factory and Singleton behavior, while Builder remains useful for complex object construction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Creational Patterns vs DI Containers
Factory Method
A @Bean method in a configuration class is effectively a factory method the container calls to obtain instances.
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
  @Bean
  public UserRepository userRepository() {
    return new JpaUserRepository();
  }
}
Singleton
Spring provides managed singletons by default, avoiding the need for a class-level getInstance call while keeping testability and configurability.
You can change scope to prototype if you need new instances each time.
Builder
Use Builder for complex object setup and then inject the built object. DI handles wiring; Builder handles complex construction detail.
Example use: configuring an HttpClient before injection into services.
Key Takeaway

DI containers often take on the role of factories and singleton managers; creational patterns still apply for specific construction tasks and configuration objects.

screens.title: Managed Singleton vs Classic Singleton
screens.narratorSegment: A classic Singleton enforces a single instance by embedding that guarantee inside the class, often using a static getInstance method. Container-managed singletons, by contrast, let the IoC container control singularity. This difference matters because managed singletons are easier to configure and test. With a container you can swap implementations, change scope through configuration, or inject a mock for testing without altering class internals. Classic singletons often couple code to static methods and global state, which makes unit testing and substitution cumbersome. A common mistake is assuming managed singletons will behave exactly like static singletons; you must still consider bean scope and thread-safety for stateful singletons. In Spring a class annotated with @Component is a singleton by default, but you can annotate it with @Scope("prototype") to request new instances for each injection. A practical example from the chapter shows how retrieving the same bean twice from the application context returns the same instance by default, and you can verify this with identity checks. The key design lesson is to prefer container-managed scope for flexibility and testability, and only use classic singletons when you truly need global, language-level guarantees.

keyIdea.title: Managed singleton
keyIdea.text: Let the container manage singularity to keep code configurable and testable rather than relying on class-enforced global state.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Managed Singleton vs Classic Singleton
Classic Singleton
A class-level pattern that keeps a single instance accessible via a static method. Harder to test and replace.
Problem: global state and tight coupling to static methods.
Container-managed Singleton
Spring creates a single bean instance by default and returns the same instance when injected or requested from context.
Benefit: swap implementations, mock in tests, and configure scope externally.
Key Takeaway

Prefer container-managed singletons for flexibility and testability; avoid static singletons when possible.

screens.title: Builder Pattern and DI
screens.narratorSegment: Although a DI container handles wiring and object lifecycle, the Builder pattern remains useful for constructing complex configuration or data objects before injection. Use a Builder when an object requires many fields or multi-step configuration that would clutter service constructors. For instance, if you need a highly configured HttpClient with timeouts, interceptors, and authentication, a Builder helps create a clear, readable construction sequence. Then you register the resulting instance as a bean and let the container inject it where needed. This separation keeps services focused on orchestration and behavior, not on the details of constructing complex dependencies. A common misuse is to try to inject many primitive configuration parameters directly into a constructor; instead group them into a configuration object built by a Builder and inject that object. The Builder also improves testability: tests can create alternative configurations easily. As a takeaway, treat DI as the wiring mechanism and Builder as a local construction tool for complex objects that are then provided by the container. Builder Pattern and DI means use builder to prepare complex objects, then inject the built object for cleaner service interfaces and better testability.. In practical terms, when to use builder for injected objects. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Builder Pattern and DI
When to use Builder
For objects with many configuration options or multi-step construction, prefer Builder then inject the built result.
Benefit: keeps service constructors small and semantically clear.
Example flow
  1. Use Builder to configure a complex client or settings object.
  2. Register the built object as a @Bean.
  3. Let the container inject the ready-to-use object into services.
Check

If a service constructor needs many primitives, refactor into a built configuration object and inject that instead.

Starter code snippets
// MessageService.java
public interface MessageService {
  String getMessage();
}

// GreetingService.java
@Component
public class GreetingService implements MessageService {
  @Override
  public String getMessage() { return "Hello from GreetingService!"; }
}

// NotificationService.java
@Component
public class NotificationService {
  private final MessageService messageService;
  public NotificationService(MessageService messageService) { this.messageService = messageService; }
  public String sendNotification() { return "Sending notification: " + messageService.getMessage(); }
}

screens.title: Hands-on Spring Boot Activity — Run and Observe
screens.narratorSegment: After you wire components, add a CommandLineRunner or simple controller to obtain NotificationService from the application context and call sendNotification. You will see console output showing the message from GreetingService. To explore scope, request NotificationService twice from the context and compare their identity. The chapter's example prints the result of equality checks and identity hash codes so you can see whether Spring returned the same instance. This demonstrates the default singleton behavior: for a given bean definition Spring creates one instance and reuses it. To change that behavior, annotate the bean with @Scope("prototype") to get a new instance each time. A common misunderstanding is assuming prototype beans always behave the same when injected into singletons — injected prototype beans become single instances inside the singleton unless you use provider or lookup injection, so be careful with scope mixing. This reinforces the testability benefit of DI: you change the wiring, not the consumer code. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Hands-on Spring Boot Activity — Run and Observe
CommandLineRunner example
@Bean
public CommandLineRunner run(ApplicationContext context) {
  return args -> {
    NotificationService s1 = context.getBean(NotificationService.class);
    System.out.println(s1.sendNotification());

    NotificationService s2 = context.getBean(NotificationService.class);
    System.out.println("Are both NotificationService instances the same? " + (s1 == s2));
    System.out.println("Hash1: " + System.identityHashCode(s1));
    System.out.println("Hash2: " + System.identityHashCode(s2));
  };
}
Observations & pitfalls
  • Default beans are singletons; the same instance is returned on repeated requests.
  • Prototype beans injected into singletons may behave unexpectedly unless proxied or provided on demand.
  • Swapping implementations requires changing configuration, not consumer classes.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Design Guidelines
screens.narratorSegment: When adopting DI it is easy to fall into habits that reduce the benefits you sought. One common mistake is over-injecting: constructors with many parameters are a sign your class has too many responsibilities and should be refactored into smaller collaborators. Another pitfall is misunderstanding bean scopes—injecting prototype-scoped beans into singletons will not magically produce new instances for each use unless you use a provider or lookup method. Field injection is convenient but makes unit testing harder because your class no longer exposes a simple constructor to supply mocks. Also be cautious with stateful singletons; if a bean holds mutable state this shared state can cause unexpected interactions across requests or components. Prefer immutable or stateless beans, or use narrower scopes where needed. A practical guideline is to prefer constructor injection for required dependencies, use setter injection sparingly for optional or mutable collaborations, and reserve field injection for framework-managed integration code where refactoring is impractical. Regularly inspect long constructors and unexpected shared state—they are early indicators that DI principles are being misapplied. Common Mistakes and Design Guidelines means avoid constructor overload, be mindful of scope interactions, and favor constructor injection to keep code testable.. In practical terms, avoid over-injecting, misuse of scopes, and field-injection traps. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Over-injecting
Long constructors often mean a class has multiple responsibilities. Refactor into smaller services.

Field injection trap
Field injection hides dependencies and complicates unit tests. Prefer constructor injection for testability.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll unpack two foundational ideas that modern Java frameworks use to keep large codebases clean and testable. Inversion of Control is a design principle where the framework, not your classes, decides when and how components are created and called. Dependency Injection is the practical mechanism that supplies an object with the other objects it needs to do its work. Together they shift responsibility for object creation to an external container, which improves modularity, simplifies testing, and reduces direct coupling between classes. You will see a concrete example with a UserService and a UserRepository, and we will contrast manual ‘new’ construction with container-managed creation. We will also explain constructor, setter, and field injection, and how DI containers map to creational patterns like Factory and Singleton so you can reason about object scope and lifecycle. By the end of this chapter you will know how DI changes where object wiring happens, why constructor injection is usually preferred, and the common pitfalls to avoid when using container-managed singletons or field injection. Consider how handing over control to a container changes the responsibilities of your classes and what that means for testing and substitutability.

By the end of this chapter you will do four practical things that matter when building maintainable Java code. First, you will define Inversion of Control and explain how moving control to a container decouples components; this helps you reason about where responsibilities belong. Second, you will understand Dependency Injection as the implementation of IoC and list its benefits such as improved testability and reduced coupling, with clear examples that show how to replace a concrete repository with a mock. Third, you will identify constructor, setter, and field injection, and describe practical trade-offs so you can choose the safest option for required versus optional dependencies. Fourth, you will explain how DI containers like Spring manage creation, injection, and lifecycle, and relate that to creational patterns like Factory and Singleton so you can predict object scope and lifecycle. Each objective equips you to make design choices and avoid common mistakes such as over-injecting or misusing singleton scope. Let's look at the competency cards you will master.

These practical objectives focus on skills you'll use immediately in a Spring-based project. You will set up a simple Spring Boot demo that uses constructor injection so you can observe how the container creates and wires beans. You will write an interface and two implementations, mark them as components, and retrieve a service from the application context to verify behavior. You will also observe default singleton scope and how to change it, and learn to detect the common mistakes that occur when you over-inject or use field injection indiscriminately. The hands-on activity in this chapter walks you step-by-step through creating MessageService, GreetingService, and NotificationService. As you complete the activity, pay attention to how swapping an implementation or changing a bean scope requires only container configuration, not changes inside consumers. This practical experience ties the conceptual ideas of IoC and DI to real code so you can design components that are easier to test and maintain.

Inversion of Control is a design principle that flips who decides what happens in your application. Instead of your classes instantiating and orchestrating every dependency, a framework or container takes responsibility for calling into your components and creating them as needed. That change in control decouples the flow of your application from the specific implementations of its parts. For example, rather than a service asking for a repository with new, the framework constructs the repository and supplies it when the service is created. This matters because it reduces the knowledge each class needs about other classes, making them easier to test and replace. A common misconception is that IoC means removing all application logic; it does not. IoC only transfers responsibility for object lifecycle and wiring to the container; domain behavior still lives in your classes. A helpful analogy is a stage production: imagine the container as the stage manager who cues actors (your components), while the actors focus on their script. Practically, IoC leads to clearer boundaries between configuration and behavior, and it enables features like lifecycle callbacks and scoped instances. Reflect on whether a class should create its own collaborators or instead expose the collaborators it needs, so the container can supply them.

Dependency Injection is a specific way to implement Inversion of Control by supplying an object's collaborators from the outside. The central claim is simple: a class should declare what it needs and let someone else provide it. That makes the class modular and easier to test. To make this concrete, compare two implementations of a UserService. In the tightly coupled version the service constructs its own UserRepository. This forces the service to know about a particular implementation and prevents easy substitution. In the injected version the UserRepository is provided in the constructor. This lets tests supply a mock implementation or swap in a different persistence strategy without changing the service. A common pitfall is over-using DI to inject too many responsibilities into a single class; if a constructor grows long, it may indicate a design problem. Another misconception is that DI removes coupling entirely — it reduces implementation coupling but introduces configuration coupling via the container. In practice DI improves maintainability: you change wiring once in the configuration rather than modifying many classes. As a takeaway, whenever a class talks about 'new' for collaborators, ask whether those collaborators belong in a container instead.

There are three widely used styles of dependency injection, and each has trade-offs you should know. Constructor injection provides dependencies through a class constructor and is preferred for required collaborators because it guarantees a fully initialized object and promotes immutability. For example, a NotificationService that requires a MessageService should declare it in the constructor so you cannot create the notification service without the message service. Setter injection supplies dependencies via public setter methods. This works well for optional dependencies or when you need to change a collaborator after construction, but it requires null checks or runtime checks to ensure correctness. Field injection places dependencies directly into private fields using framework support, for example with annotations in Spring. It is concise but reduces testability because it bypasses constructors and setters, making manual instantiation harder. A common misconception is that field injection is always fine for small projects; in unit testing scenarios constructor injection reduces setup complexity. Also avoid 'constructor hell' where a single class has many constructor parameters—this is usually a symptom that the class has too many responsibilities. As a takeaway, prefer constructor injection for required dependencies, setter injection for optional ones, and reserve field injection for framework-managed components where constructor wiring is impractical.

A DI container performs four essential responsibilities that shape how your application behaves. First, it creates object instances for classes registered as beans or components. Second, it resolves dependencies by inspecting constructor parameters, setter methods, or field annotations and determining which beans satisfy those contracts. Third, it injects resolved dependencies into the target objects so the objects can operate without creating their own collaborators. Fourth, it manages object lifecycle, which includes singleton default scope, optional prototype scope, and lifecycle callbacks like initialization and destruction. These responsibilities map directly to creational patterns: the container behaves like a central Factory that decides when to call factory methods or construct objects, and like a managed Singleton registry when it provides a single shared instance for a bean. A common misunderstanding is that the container replaces design patterns; instead, it complements them by centralizing creation and reducing boilerplate. Practically, knowing these responsibilities helps you predict when objects are instantiated, when shared state might occur, and how to configure scopes to avoid unintended sharing. When designing components, assume the container will construct and wire them, and keep classes focused on behavior rather than creation.

Creational patterns remain useful even when you adopt DI, but a container often takes over their roles. The Factory Method pattern encapsulates object creation in a method; when you annotate @Bean or use configuration, the container calls a factory method on your behalf. The Singleton pattern enforces a single instance at the class level, but a DI container provides a more flexible managed singleton: the container controls singularity and can swap implementations for testing. The Builder pattern still applies when constructing complex value or configuration objects; the container can inject a fully built object rather than assembling it itself. A common misconception is that DI obviates these patterns entirely; instead DI often reduces boilerplate by centralizing creation while the patterns remain the right tool for constructing particular object families or complex instances. For example, a @Configuration class that defines a userRepository bean is conceptually a factory method. If you need a complex HttpClient, using a Builder to configure it before injection keeps your services simple and the configuration explicit. As a takeaway, view the container as an orchestrator that can call your factory methods and manage scopes, allowing creational patterns and DI to complement each other.

A classic Singleton enforces a single instance by embedding that guarantee inside the class, often using a static getInstance method. Container-managed singletons, by contrast, let the IoC container control singularity. This difference matters because managed singletons are easier to configure and test. With a container you can swap implementations, change scope through configuration, or inject a mock for testing without altering class internals. Classic singletons often couple code to static methods and global state, which makes unit testing and substitution cumbersome. A common mistake is assuming managed singletons will behave exactly like static singletons; you must still consider bean scope and thread-safety for stateful singletons. In Spring a class annotated with @Component is a singleton by default, but you can annotate it with @Scope("prototype") to request new instances for each injection. A practical example from the chapter shows how retrieving the same bean twice from the application context returns the same instance by default, and you can verify this with identity checks. The key design lesson is to prefer container-managed scope for flexibility and testability, and only use classic singletons when you truly need global, language-level guarantees.

Although a DI container handles wiring and object lifecycle, the Builder pattern remains useful for constructing complex configuration or data objects before injection. Use a Builder when an object requires many fields or multi-step configuration that would clutter service constructors. For instance, if you need a highly configured HttpClient with timeouts, interceptors, and authentication, a Builder helps create a clear, readable construction sequence. Then you register the resulting instance as a bean and let the container inject it where needed. This separation keeps services focused on orchestration and behavior, not on the details of constructing complex dependencies. A common misuse is to try to inject many primitive configuration parameters directly into a constructor; instead group them into a configuration object built by a Builder and inject that object. The Builder also improves testability: tests can create alternative configurations easily. As a takeaway, treat DI as the wiring mechanism and Builder as a local construction tool for complex objects that are then provided by the container. Finally, keep a short checklist for practice: prefer constructor injection for required dependencies because it ensures valid object state and improves testability; use setter injection for optional collaborators; avoid field injection when you need easy unit tests. Remember that the DI container often acts like a Factory and a managed Singleton registry, so configure bean scopes consciously to avoid unwanted shared state. Watch out for constructor hell where many parameters indicate a design smell, and for mixing singleton and prototype scopes without proper providers. In testing, swap implementations through configuration rather than editing consumer classes. These practical rules will help you apply IoC and DI correctly, keeping components focused and easy to test. As a closing question: which injection style would you choose for a required, stateful collaborator and why?
